person.name: Alan_Turing
person.summary: Alan Turing gave a mathematical account of general computation and helped break German naval Enigma messages during World War II. He later designed early computer systems, proposed a test for machine intelligence, and developed a mathematical explanation for biological pattern formation.

conclusion: Alan Turing gave computer science a formal way to describe what machines can calculate and what no general method can decide. His wartime work helped British codebreakers read German naval Enigma traffic. His ideas about machine intelligence and biological patterns continue to guide research.

events.title: Birth in Maida Vale
events.description: His father, Julius Mathison Turing, served in the [[Indian Civil Service]] and was home in England on leave. His mother, Ethel Sara Turing, came from a Protestant Anglo-Irish family with ties to engineering and public administration. Alan joined his older brother John in a family whose parents traveled between India and England.

Indian Civil Service.explanation: The Indian Civil Service was the senior civil administration of British India. Julius Turing served in the Madras Presidency.

events.title: Enters Sherborne School
events.description: Turing entered Sherborne School in Dorset as a boarder after attending Hazelhurst Preparatory School. The first day of term coincided with the British General Strike. He bicycled about 60 miles from Southampton to reach the school and continued to pursue mathematics and science there.

events.title: Loses Christopher Morcom
events.description: Christopher Collan Morcom died in February 1930 from complications of [[bovine tuberculosis]]. Turing was a pupil at Sherborne School and wrote to Morcom's mother, Frances Isobel Morcom. He worked more intensely on the mathematics and science that he and Morcom had shared.

bovine tuberculosis.explanation: Bovine tuberculosis is an infectious disease caused by bacteria that primarily affect cattle. People could contract it through infected milk.

events.background:
Sherborne School treated the classics as the center of a proper education. Several teachers had little use for Turing's preference for mathematics and science. His headmaster warned his parents that a student who became solely a scientific specialist was wasting his time at a public school. Turing nevertheless worked through advanced problems in 1927 before learning elementary calculus. At sixteen he read Albert Einstein's work and may have inferred Einstein's challenge to Newton's laws of motion from a text that left it unstated. In this setting, Christopher Morcom offered an intellectual companionship that Turing did not find elsewhere. Morcom introduced him to astronomy. Turing later called him brilliant, charming, and unpretentious.

The friendship gave Turing a person with whom to share his interests in scientific work. In his letter to Frances Morcom, he said that he had regarded his work and astronomy as subjects to share with Christopher. He believed Christopher had felt something similar. The letter also set a demanding rule for his own work. Turing wrote that he must put into it as much energy, if not the same interest, as he would if Christopher were alive. He thought that was what Christopher would have wanted.

Turing continued writing to Frances Morcom for years. The correspondence included gifts from her and letters from him, especially around Christopher's birthday. On February 12, 1933, the day before the third anniversary, he wrote that he would be thinking of both Christopher and Frances the following day. In another letter, he considered whether a spirit could survive bodily death. He wrote that matter and spirit were eternally connected, though he could not say what happened during sleep. He imagined that death ended the bodily mechanism holding a spirit, after which the spirit found a new body. Later observers have connected the loss with Turing's atheism and materialism. The article says that, at this point, he still entertained ideas of a spirit independent of the body.

events.title: Studies at King's College
events.description: Turing began studying mathematics at King’s College, Cambridge, on a scholarship in February 1931. His dissertation on the Gaussian error function proved a version of the [[central limit theorem]]. He completed the course with first-class honors in 1934.

central limit theorem.explanation: The central limit theorem describes how averages of many independent observations tend to follow a normal, bell-shaped distribution under broad conditions. Turing’s dissertation proved a version of this result using the Gaussian error function.

events.title: Studies at Princeton
events.description: In September 1936, Turing left Cambridge, England, for Princeton University in Princeton, New Jersey, where he studied under Alonzo Church. He pursued doctoral research in [[ordinal logic|ordinal logic]], built an electromechanical binary multiplier, and completed his doctorate in June 1938.

images.caption: Alan Turing at Princeton University in 1936
images.creator: Unknown photographer

ordinal logic.explanation: Ordinal logic extends formal mathematical systems by adding axioms through successive finite and transfinite stages indexed by ordinal numbers. Turing studied this approach in his Princeton dissertation.

events.title: Publishes Computable Numbers
events.description: Turing published On Computable Numbers, with an Application to the [[Entscheidungsproblem]] in November 1936. Before leaving Cambridge, he had sent an early draft to Max Newman. The paper introduced the [[universal computing machine|universal computing machine]], a machine that can carry out the operations of any other computing machine. It proved that no general method can solve the Entscheidungsproblem.

images.caption: Turing machine, associated with Computable Numbers
images.creator: User:Wvbailey

universal computing machine.explanation: A universal computing machine is a theoretical machine that can imitate any other computing machine when given its instructions. Turing used the concept to describe computation in general terms.

Entscheidungsproblem.explanation: The Entscheidungsproblem asked whether a general method could determine the logical validity of every statement in a formal system. Turing proved that no such method exists.

event_class.title: On Computable Numbers, with an Application to the Entscheidungsproblem
event_class.publisher: Proceedings of the London Mathematical Society
event_class.impact: The paper established a formal model of general computation and proved that no general algorithm can solve the Entscheidungsproblem.

events.background:
At Cambridge, Max Newman’s 1935 lectures on the foundations of mathematics and Gödel’s theorem gave students a live problem left by David Hilbert and Wilhelm Ackermann in 1928. Gödel had established limits on formal systems. Turing began investigating whether a procedure could settle every question of the kind Hilbert had posed. He worked on the problem from the spring of 1935 through 1936 while completing Part III of the Mathematical Tripos. Alonzo Church reached a related conclusion through lambda calculus. Church’s article appeared in April 1936, when Turing’s work was still in draft.

Turing made his argument depend on deliberately spare imaginary devices. Each had a tape divided into squares, a read-and-write head, and a finite table of instructions governing its next move. He gave every machine a standard description made from a small alphabet of symbols. The description could also be converted into an octal number. That pairing let the argument treat instructions as data that another machine could inspect.

The central construction assumed a deciding machine called D. D would classify the descriptions of machines according to whether they continued printing binary digits without end. A second machine, H, would use D to examine descriptions one by one. H would simulate each successful machine long enough to copy a selected digit onto its own tape. The resulting diagonal sequence would have to differ from every sequence in H’s list. Yet H itself belonged among the machines being classified. The contradiction came from the assumed existence of D.

Newman recognized the importance of Turing’s draft and helped secure rapid publication. Turing finished the 36-page manuscript on May 28, 1936. Its two parts appeared on November 30 and December 23. Newman also arranged Turing’s visit to Princeton, where Church was working on the same question. John von Neumann later credited the paper’s central idea as the basis of the modern computer.

events.title: Joins Bletchley Park
events.description: On 4 September 1939, the day after Britain declared war on Germany, Alan Turing reported to [[Bletchley Park|Bletchley Park]], the wartime center of the [[Government Code and Cypher School|British codebreaking organization]]. He began working with Dilly Knox on [[Enigma machine|German Enigma communications]], signing the Official Secrets Act as he joined the secret effort.

images.caption: Bletchley Park Mansion, wartime codebreaking headquarters
images.creator: DeFacto

Bletchley Park.explanation: Bletchley Park was the British wartime codebreaking center where the Government Code and Cypher School analyzed intercepted enemy communications.

Government Code and Cypher School.explanation: The Government Code and Cypher School was Britain's codebreaking organization during World War II. It later became the Government Communications Headquarters.

Enigma machine.explanation: The Enigma machine was a German cipher device that encrypted military and government messages. Turing and other codebreakers developed methods to recover its settings and read the messages.

events.title: Designs the Bombe
events.description: In early 1940 at Bletchley Park, Turing specified the British bombe, an electromechanical machine that searched possible Enigma settings. Gordon Welchman added the diagonal board, which made the search more efficient. The design built on earlier work by Polish cryptanalysts against German Enigma messages.

images.caption: A Turing Bombe at Bletchley Park
images.creator: Ian Petticrew

event_class.title: Turing bombe
event_class.description: An electromechanical machine tests Enigma rotor settings against a suspected message fragment and rejects settings that create logical contradictions.
event_class.impact: Bombes gave Bletchley Park a practical way to recover Enigma settings quickly enough for wartime intelligence work.

events.background:
Before the war, the Government Code and Cypher School had studied commercial Enigma machines. In July 1939, Polish cryptanalysts met British and French representatives near Warsaw and disclosed their work on the German system. Their bomba relied on an indicator procedure that German operators changed in May 1940. Turing and Dilly Knox developed a broader approach based on cribs, short pieces of likely plaintext in an intercepted message. A message ending with a routine weather report or a standard military phrase could supply such a clue.

The first British bombe entered service on March 18, 1940. Its searches depended on a crib and on the internal connections implied by an Enigma message. Enigma could never turn a letter into itself. The machine used that rule to discard impossible settings. Welchman’s diagonal board used the plugboard’s reciprocal wiring. A plugboard connection from B to G necessarily also connected G to B. The board allowed the plugboard connections to be solved separately from the rotor settings. Complete settings could then be found in hours after previously requiring days.

By late 1941, the codebreakers had a working system, though too few staff members and bombes to read every signal. Turing, Welchman, Hugh Alexander, and Stuart Milner-Barry wrote directly to Winston Churchill on October 28. They asked for people and machines after ordinary channels had failed. Churchill sent General Ismay an “Action This Day” instruction to give the work extreme priority. More than two hundred bombes were operating by the end of the war. Welchman later supervised their construction, deployment, and operation, and coordinated with the United States so British and American machines did not work on the same keys.

events.title: Leads Hut 8
events.description: In 1940, Turing took charge of Hut 8, the Bletchley Park section responsible for German naval Enigma traffic. He worked with Joan Clarke and other cryptanalysts on naval messages. He developed Banburismus, a statistical method that reduced the number of Enigma settings that bombes needed to test as the German Navy strengthened protection for U-boat communications.

images.caption: Banbury sheet used in Turing's Banburismus
images.creator: TedColes

events.title: Designs the Automatic Computing Engine
events.description: In October 1945, Turing joined the National Physical Laboratory, a government research laboratory in London, after completing his wartime work. He drafted plans for the Automatic Computing Engine, an electronic stored-program computer. The design aimed to make his ideas about general-purpose computation practical.

images.caption: Pilot ACE computer at the Science Museum
images.creator: Antoine Taveneaux

event_class.title: Automatic Computing Engine
event_class.description: A stored-program electronic computer design used high-speed electronic memory to hold instructions and numerical data for general calculations.
event_class.impact: Its design influenced British computer engineering and informed later work on practical stored-program machines.

events.title: Moves to Manchester
events.description: In May 1948, Alan Turing left London for Manchester to join Max Newman’s Computing Machine Laboratory at the University of Manchester. There, Turing worked with Frederic Williams and Tom Kilburn on the [[Manchester Baby|Manchester Baby]], an early stored-program computer, and its successor, the Manchester Mark I.

images.caption: Manchester University SSEM Baby replica
images.creator: Users Ian Dunster, Racklever on en.wikipedia

Manchester Baby.explanation: The Manchester Baby was the first working stored-program electronic computer. Built at the University of Manchester in 1948, it tested Williams and Kilburn’s memory system and supported the laboratory’s early computer research.

events.title: Creates Turochamp
events.description: In 1948, Turing and his former King’s College friend David Champernowne devised Turochamp, a program for playing chess. They worked at the University of Manchester. No available computer could run the program at a useful speed.

images.caption: Chess game calculated by the TUROCHAMP program
images.creator: Morn

event_class.title: Turochamp
event_class.description: A chess-playing algorithm evaluates candidate moves with rules for material, mobility, threats, and positional advantage.
event_class.impact: It became one of the earliest designs for a computer chess program.

events.title: Proposes the Imitation Game
events.description: In October 1950, Turing published Computing Machinery and Intelligence in Mind. The paper proposed the [[Imitation Game|Imitation Game]], in which a human judge communicates by text with a person and a computer and tries to distinguish between them.

Imitation Game.explanation: The Imitation Game is Turing's proposed practical test for machine intelligence. It later became widely known as the Turing test.

event_class.title: Computing Machinery and Intelligence
event_class.impact: The imitation game became known as the Turing test and remains a reference point in debates about machine intelligence.

events.background:
British researchers had discussed machine intelligence for almost a decade before the field acquired the name artificial intelligence in 1956. The Ratio Club, an informal circle of cybernetics and electronics researchers, treated the subject as a common concern. Turing had been considering it by 1941 and used the phrase “computer intelligence” in 1947. His work at the University of Manchester also put the question beside actual early digital computers, whose speed and memory were still sharply limited.

The paper narrowed its attention to digital machinery. Such machines stored and rewrote binary digits, 1 and 0, by fixed rules. Turing argued that a digital computer with enough storage, speed, and an appropriate program could simulate any other digital machine. He therefore framed the issue around the capacities of an imaginable future machine, not the performance of the few machines then available. The discussion joined a practical account of computing to questions usually handled by philosophers, including what people mean when they call something intelligent.

Turing devoted much of the paper to nine anticipated objections. One came from Ada Lovelace’s claim that the Analytical Engine could only carry out instructions supplied by its programmer. He answered that machines could produce results that surprised their programmers. He also addressed arguments based on consciousness, the limits of formal mathematics, the apparent informality of human behavior, and extrasensory perception. He gave a dated forecast for the new criterion. He expected that by about 2000, a machine with roughly 10^9 units of storage would allow an average interrogator only a 70 percent chance of making the right identification after five minutes of questioning. The question continued into philosophy of artificial intelligence, where John Searle’s Chinese room argument became one prominent criticism.

events.title: Convicted in Manchester
events.description: On March 31, 1952, a court in Manchester convicted Turing of [[gross indecency]] after he reported a burglary involving Arnold Murray. The charge criminalized sexual acts between men. Turing accepted a year of [[chemical castration|hormone treatment]], an alternative to imprisonment.

images.caption: Facade of Manchester County Court Offices
images.creator: Anthony Parkes

gross indecency.explanation: “Gross indecency” was a criminal offense used in the United Kingdom to prosecute sexual acts between men.

chemical castration.explanation: Chemical castration uses hormone treatment to reduce sexual drive. Turing accepted it for one year as an alternative to prison.

events.title: Explains Biological Patterns
events.description: Turing published The Chemical Basis of Morphogenesis in 1952. The paper described a [[reaction-diffusion|reaction-diffusion system]] in which chemicals react and spread through tissue. The model explained how patterns such as stripes and spirals can arise from an initially uniform state.

reaction-diffusion.explanation: A reaction-diffusion system describes substances that change through local chemical reactions while spreading through space. Turing used this model to account for regular patterns in developing organisms.

event_class.title: The Chemical Basis of Morphogenesis
event_class.publisher: Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society
event_class.impact: The paper established reaction-diffusion models as a major approach to studying biological pattern formation.

events.background:
At the University of Manchester, Turing worked in Max Newman’s Computing Machine Laboratory after the war and contributed to its early computers. His attention then turned to mathematical biology. The new subject asked how an embryo could acquire organized features while developing from material that initially appeared uniform. His work brought the methods of mathematical analysis into a field concerned with animal coats, skin pigmentation, and the growth of living structures.

The argument treated pattern formation as a problem that could be expressed with nonlinear partial differential equations. Such equations track change across space and time. They can produce fronts, spirals, targets, hexagons, and stripes under different local chemical conditions. The same general framework remained open to analytical treatment even when the local reactions differed greatly. That made it useful to theorists studying visible biological forms.

Turing also predicted oscillating chemical reactions. The Belousov–Zhabotinsky reaction, an example of such chemical oscillation, was first observed during the 1960s. Later researchers applied Turing-pattern ideas to particular developmental questions. One proposal holds that the protein VEGFC can form such patterns during the growth of lymphatic vessels in zebrafish embryos. Reaction–diffusion processes have also remained one explanation used in studies of embryonic animal-coat development and skin pigmentation.

events.title: Death in Wilmslow
events.description: The 1952 conviction had cost Turing his security clearance. The court had ordered a year of hormone treatment. He lived alone in Wilmslow. His housekeeper found him dead in bed.
